extracted.intended_audience: architects, sculptors, decorative artists, and students of architectural ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for selecting materials, subjects, and treatments for architectural ornament and sculpture, with rules about when human-made objects may be used and which natural forms are appropriate. Emphasizes subordinate relationship of ornament to figure-subject and the use of nature-derived lines and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human work inadmissible as independent ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: On no terms whatever could any such subject (human manufacture/work) be independently admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The permission to represent human work as an ornament is conditional on its necessity to represent a scene or explain an action; otherwise carving our own work for admiration is 'miserable self-complacency'. Human-made subjects (heraldries, king's arms, manifestations of civic or invented laws) are base as ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for representing manufacture as ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the use of manufacture as ornament is — 1. With heroic figure sculpture, not admissible at all. 2. With picturesque figure sculpture, admissible in the degree of its picturesqueness. 3. Without figure sculpture, not admissible at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human manufacture may only appear when it serves explanation of a scene and in proportion to the picturesqueness of the figure-subject; it must not be independent or prominent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture as ornament must be subordinated
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture itself may be introduced as an explanation of the scene in which the figures act; but with more or less prominence in the inverse ratio of the importance of the figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where figures are of great value/beauty, it is an impertinence to disturb contemplation by minor architectural features. If figures are life-size and complete statues, carving a temple above them or distributing them over sculptured rocks is 'gross vulgarity'. For bas-relief, architectural scenery should be 'lightly traced outlines'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipping and manufactured objects: subordinate, not realized
rubrics_metrics.description: Shipping (and other human products) may be introduced only in severe subordination to the figure-subject and only sketched in the lightest lines on the background; never with any attempt at realisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ship may be introduced just enough to indicate the scene but not equal in force or realism to the figures unless the whole purpose is partly picturesque (i.e., the subject purposely derives enjoyment from accidents rather than the heart of the thing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracted details (e.g., cable) acceptable, literal copies are not
rubrics_metrics.description: The cable as ornament is not the cable itself, but its abstract form, a group of twisted lines which is indeed beautiful as an ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the resemblance complete (give stone the threads and character of a cable) and you may view it with curiosity but not admiration. Use abstracted form rather than literal, minute replication of human artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of ornament: to make you happy by showing divine work
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of ornament is to make you happy; you are to be made happy by ornaments; therefore they must be the expression of man's delight in God's work, not copies of your own handiwork or boastings of your own grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects and treatments that express natural/divine laws and delights (not heraldry, king's arms, or civic self-congratulation). Ornament should celebrate creation and its laws rather than human inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper material for ornament: what God has created
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper material of ornament will be whatever God has created; and its proper treatment, that which seems in accordance with or symbolical of His laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select materials and motifs drawn from natural forms (abstract lines, elements, organisms) rather than human manufacture; treat them in manners corresponding to their natural character and symbolic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract lines as first constituent of ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Our first constituents of ornament will therefore be abstract lines, that is to say, the most frequent contours of natural objects, transferred to architectural forms when it is not right or possible to render such forms distinctly imitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract shadows and colors are matters of treatment not selection; use contours (curves) from nature. Prefer natural stone tints for coloring. For general decorative work, be content with a few simple, serviceable curves (e.g., one mountain line and one leaf line).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple transferable curves over refined natural curves
rubrics_metrics.description: We need not hope to imitate the subtly combined curvatures of nature's highest designing; their extreme refinement renders them unfit for coarse service or material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lines lovely in a shell or distant hills are lost in stone; therefore choose simpler fragments of natural curves (e.g., a mountain fragment and a leaf fragment) for ornament in stone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use crystals and geometric inorganic forms freely
rubrics_metrics.description: Against crystalline form (the systematised natural structure of the earth) objections do not hold good, and accordingly it is an endless element of decoration where higher conditions cannot be represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pyramids (dogtooth), cubes, rhombs, chequers, dentils, and mouldings derived from crystalline habits as durable decorative motifs rather than attempting to copy rocks or mountains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not imitate rocks and mountains literally
rubrics_metrics.description: The nobility of rocks and mountains depends on scale and accident; their scale cannot be represented nor their accident systematised, so literal imitation is unwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitations of rock form are mostly signs of degraded feeling (grottoes, garden features, Calvaries); only use actual untouched blocks for rough service or general mountain-structure examples, not delicate imitation of accidental fracture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of water: use conventional undulatory types
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptors have been forced to invent types/letters for water — undulatory lines often with fish to indicate water; types range from conventional zigzag to naturalistic attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer conventional undulatory lines (the established types) and fish to explain water; where imitation is attempted, edge waves clearly and express foam with drill-holes or other devices rather than vapid, joyless portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of fire: use radiation symbolically and sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire is hardly manageable and has been symbolised by radiation both in painting and sculpture, mostly unsuccessfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radiation motifs and flame imitations (torches, burning urn-tops, gilded rays) are of limited ornamental use and often poor in execution; treat with caution or leave to less reputable decorative fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of air (clouds) are scale- and color-dependent; trace lightly
rubrics_metrics.description: Clouds are hardly manageable and of no ornamental use except by scale and color; they are inimitable in marble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If used, represent clouds lightly (as in some Cinquecento sculpture) or boldly where appropriate (e.g., Last Judgment porches), but avoid heavy, elaborate imitations in stone that seek to reproduce scale or color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shells and shell-forms: use lines, not bulk
rubrics_metrics.description: Shells are moulds or coats of organisms and their sense of emptiness prevents large use in ornamentation; better to take the line and leave the shell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shell-lines for half-domes (conchas) and radiant forms (scallops) sparingly and combined with other symbols; avoid portraying shells as empty bulk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish as valuable ornamental material and symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Fish are beautiful in form and symbolically meaningful; simple fish forms are widely used in medieval work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose supple forms with scaly bodies and lashing tails for picturesqueness, or plain oval-bodied types where appropriate (e.g., Thunny at Venice); Greek dolphin types are particularly picturesque and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reptiles and insects: combine beauty with horror for pictorial effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of serpent and lizard exhibit elements of beauty and horror and have been favourite subjects in all periods of art; ideal dragons combine unity of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use serpents/dragons with symbolic intent in medieval picturesque sculpture; avoid mere meaningless interlaced representations except where symbol or effect justifies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular curves signify rest/support; other curves signify action
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all the natural lines described are expressive of action or force, while the circle is a line of limitation or support; circular curves are appropriate as signs of rest and support (e.g., arches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use circular curves in structural/supporting features (arches) and use action-expressive curves in active architectural features (capitals, bases) and minor ornaments, more freely where structural independence allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color and shadow are matters of treatment, not selection
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no abstract shadows or colors irrespective of the forms which exhibit them; arrangement of shadows and color masses is treatment, not selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using color in architecture, natural stone tints are safest and rarely offensive; painted buildings are rarely quite right. Treat color and shadow to harmonise with material and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament must be explanatory when introducing human or manufactured forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Permission to represent human work as ornament is conditional on its being necessary to the representation of a scene or explanation of an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never admit manufactured subjects for their own sake; they may only appear to explain narrative content or to serve a representational necessity within the composition.
